arXiv:2510.13651v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2025

What is the objective of reasoning with reinforcement learning?

Damek Davis ††thanks: Department of Statistics and Data Science, The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania; www.damekdavis.com. Work supported by NSF DMS award 2047637.    Benjamin Recht ††thanks: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences, University of California, Berkeley https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~brecht/.
Abstract

We show that several popular algorithms for reinforcement learning in large language models with binary rewards can be viewed as stochastic gradient ascent on a monotone transform of the probability of a correct answer given a prompt. In particular, the transformation associated with rejection sampling algorithms is the logarithm and that associated with the GRPO algorithm is the arcsine of the square root.

1 Introduction

Though traditionally associated with sophisticated tree search and approximate dynamic programming, reinforcement learning takes on a unique character in the post-training of large language models. As a tool for adjusting models to align with human preferences or gain proficiency in certain test-taking domains, reinforcement learning algorithms tend to all work like the following meta-algorithm:

  1. 1.

    Sample a bunch of prompts from a corpus.

  2. 2.

    Have the model generate a set of responses to the prompts.

  3. 3.

    Have some external source, be it crowd workers or a verification engine, label the answers as good or bad.

  4. 4.

    Fine-tune the model based on the triples of prompts, responses, and labels.

We will refer to this underspecified procedure as Meta-Algorithm 1.

Many algorithms have been proposed that run some sort of variant of the meta-algorithm (see references [8-621]). In this note, we argue that they can all be interpreted as stochastic gradient methods on closely related objective functions. Namely, they aim to find a model that maximizes a monotonically increasing function of the probability of getting a correct answer conditioned on the prompt.

This serves as a unifying, simple way to look at reinforcement learning applied to large language models and to compare different algorithms. Williams’ REINFORCE algorithm and other policy gradient algorithms have enough degrees of freedom that understanding what they do when applied to particular optimization problems is not always transparent. When applied to LLMs, different implementations of Meta-algorithm 1 can all be viewed as maximizing closely related objective functions.

Moreover, Meta-algorithm 1 highlights that the base model must already perform nontrivially in order for fine tuning on correct answers alone to be profitable. If neither the base model nor the engineer can generate correct answers, then the fine-tuning algorithms cannot make progress. No sophisticated implementation of policy gradient can circumvent this constraint.

In what follows, after recalling some facts from supervised and reinforcement learning, we present a precise form of Meta-Algorithm 1 in Section 3, which aims to maximize the scaled probability of correct responses to prompts via stochastic gradient ascent. We then proceed to show how popular post-training algorithms like REINFORCE, rejection sampling fine-tuning, and GRPO are all special cases of our proposed stochastic gradient method.

2 Background: Supervised Learning and Williams’ REINFORCE algorithm.

It’s first worth reminding ourselves of what a supervised learning update looks like for probabilistic modeling. Say our goal is to fit a conditional distribution pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) to a set of nn example input-output pairs (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}). A popular approach to this problem maximizes the global objective function

∑i=1nlog⁡pθ​(yi|xi).\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log p_{\theta}(y_{i}|x_{i})\,. (2.1)

One can motivate this as seeking the maximum likelihood θ\theta given the observed input-output data. A stochastic gradient of this loss for example ii is thus

∇θ​log​pθ​(yi|xi)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(y_{i}|x_{i})

We note this because this quantity will appear throughout this work. Most of reinforcement learning when applied to LLMs looks like supervised learning, with the catch that the outputs yiy_{i} are generated by the model being optimized.

Let’s see how reinforcement learning updates relate to these supervised learning updates. To get there, we review Williams’ REINFORCE algorithm (Williams, 1992) in full generality. REINFORCE is based on the following straightforward observation. Let pθ​(z)p_{\theta}(z) be a probability distribution in zz. Define the function

Φ⁡(θ)=𝔼z∼pθ​(⋅)​[F⁡(z)].\Phi(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot)}[F(z)]\,.

Then for zz sampled from pθp_{\theta}

F⁡(z)​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(z)F(z)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(z) (2.2)

is an unbiased estimate of ∇θΦ​(θ)\nabla_{\theta}\Phi(\theta). The REINFORCE algorithm is the stochastic gradient method where the gradient estimate is the concatenation of the unbiased partial derivative estimates of (2.2).

The key to deriving this expression is the trivial equality from calculus

∇θ​log​pθ​(z)=∇θpθ​(z)pθ​(z).\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(z)=\frac{\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}(z)}{p_{\theta}(z)}\,.

Hence, by multiplying and dividing gradients of probability distributions, we can derive stochastic gradients that are proportional to the gradients of the logarithms of densities. We will make use of such analyses throughout.

The REINFORCE algorithm is general, and the distribution pθ​(⋅)p_{\theta}(\cdot) does not need to be a conditional distribution like it is in supervised learning. However, reinforcement learning applied to problems of the form

maximize∑i=1n𝔼y∼pθ(⋅|xi)[R(y,xi)].\text{maximize}~~\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{i})}[R(y,x_{i})]\,.

will have updates that look like supervised learning when the rewards are binary valued. We will explore several examples of this in the next sections.

3 Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning

Consider the simplest RL problem for large language models. We have a base model πθ\pi_{\theta} from which we can generate answers, yy, to questions, xx. Here xx functions as the prompt and yy, the response, is a random sample from a probability distribution πθ(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x), where θ\theta denotes the parameters of the probabilistic model. We assume that we have some computational means of determining when an answer yy is a “correct” response to the question xx. For each question xx, we denote the set of correct answers by C⁡(x)C(x).

The goal is to fine-tune the probabilistic model πθ\pi_{\theta} so that it frequently correctly answers questions from a corpus of questions QQ. In what follows, we show how several different versions of Meta-Algorithm 1 can be interpreted as performing stochastic gradient ascent on the objective

Jh​(θ):=𝔼x∼Q​[h⁡(∑y∈C⁡(x)πθ​(y∣x))],\displaystyle J_{h}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim Q}\left[h\left(\sum_{y\in C(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\right)\right]\,, (3.1)

for some monotonically increasing function hh. The term

pθ​(C|x):=∑y∈C⁡(x)πθ​(y∣x)p_{\theta}(C|x):=\sum_{y\in C(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x) (3.2)

is the probability a sample from πθ(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) is labeled as correct.

In practice, Meta-Algorithm 1 is implemented through the following more concrete instantiation, which we call Algorithm 1, because we refuse to come up with a cutesy, impenetrable four letter acronym.

  1. 1.

    Select a question xx from the corpus QQ.

  2. 2.

    Sample MM answers from the current model.

  3. 3.

    Based on the evaluation of each response yiy_{i}, compute a per-sample weight ZiZ_{i}.

  4. 4.

    Fine-tune the model with a supervised learning update

    θ←θ+η​1M​∑i=1MZi​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(yi∣x).\displaystyle\theta\leftarrow\theta+\eta\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}Z_{i}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x)\,. (3.3)

The weights ZiZ_{i} are often called advantages in the RL literature. Typically, algorithm designers motivate the choice of ZiZ_{i} by appealing to variance reduction. Instead, we show that typical choices of ZiZ_{i} in fact induce different cost functions hMh_{M} such that

𝔼y1:M[1M∑i=1MZi∇θlogπθ(yi∣x)]:=∇θhM(pθ(C∣x))\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y_{1:M}}\left[\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}Z_{i}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x)\right]:=\nabla_{\theta}h_{M}(p_{\theta}(C\mid x)) (3.4)

This means that our choice of advantage determines the objective JhJ_{h} in (3.1) that we optimize. For example, Williams’ version of REINFORCE, affectionately dubbed “vanilla” REINFORCE, uses advantage Zi=1yi∈C⁡(x)Z_{i}=1_{y_{i}\in C(x)} which clearly leads to objective h⁡(t)=th(t)=t. That is, it attempts to maximize the probability of correct answers, averaged over the questions.

More interestingly, we will show that using rejection sampling to find correct answers corresponds to a function close to h⁡(t)=log⁡(t)h(t)=\log(t). In addition, the popular algorithm GRPO algorithm corresponds to an objective close to h⁡(t)=arcsin⁡(t)h(t)=\arcsin(\sqrt{t}). We also ask the converse question: given a function hh, how should we choose the weights ZiZ_{i} so that the induced hMh_{M} is close to hh. It turns out the answer is related to the Bernstein polynomial expansion of hh; we discuss this in Section 7.

4 Which functions do the reweightings induce?

We will consider a specific family of weights ZiZ_{i} which are conditionally linear in RiR_{i}. Specifically, define rewards Ri=1yi∈C⁡(x)R_{i}=1_{y_{i}\in C(x)} and the leave-one-out total rewards Si=∑j≠iRiS_{i}=\sum_{j\neq i}R_{i}. The weights we consider in this work are all of the form:

Zi=(1−Ri)​aSi+Ri​bSi\displaystyle Z_{i}=(1-R_{i})a_{S_{i}}+R_{i}b_{S_{i}} (4.1)

where s↦ass\mapsto a_{s} and s↦bss\mapsto b_{s} are arbitrary (measurable) functions of ss. We claim that that such weights always induce a transform of the form.

hM​(t)=1M​∑s=0M−1(bs−as)​It​(s+1,M−s),\displaystyle h_{M}(t)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{s=0}^{M-1}(b_{s}-a_{s})I_{t}(s+1,M-s), (4.2)

where t↦It​(s+1,M−s)t\mapsto I_{t}(s+1,M-s) is the regularized incomplete beta function.

To prove this, note that each term Zi​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(yi∣x)Z_{i}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x) has the same distribution. Therefore, we must only show

𝔼yi∼πθ(⋅∣x)[Zi∇θlogπθ(yi∣x)]=∇θhM(pθ(C∣x))=hM′(pθ(C∣x))∇θpθ(C∣x).\mathbb{E}_{y_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[Z_{i}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x)\right]=\nabla_{\theta}h_{M}(p_{\theta}(C\mid x))=h_{M}^{\prime}(p_{\theta}(C\mid x))\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}(C\mid x).

We can argue this by conditioning on Si=sS_{i}=s. Indeed, fix ss, define a scalar ϕs:=bs−as\phi_{s}:=b_{s}-a_{s}, and define a function gs​(y)g_{s}(y) which is equal to bsb_{s} when y∈C⁡(x)y\in C(x) and equal to asa_{s} when y∉C⁡(x)y\notin C(x). Then conditioned on Si=sS_{i}=s, we have gs​(y)=Zig_{s}(y)=Z_{i}. Moreover, since yiy_{i} is independent of SiS_{i},

𝔼⁡[Zi​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(yi∣x)∣Si=s]=∑ygs​(y)​∇θπθ​(y∣x)=ϕs​∑y∈C⁡(x)∇θπθ​(y∣x)=ϕs​∇θpθ​(C∣x),\mathbb{E}\left[Z_{i}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x)\mid S_{i}=s\right]=\sum_{y}g_{s}(y)\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)=\phi_{s}\sum_{y\in C(x)}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)=\phi_{s}\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}(C\mid x),

Averaging over Si∼Bin⁡(M−1,p)S_{i}\sim\mathrm{Bin}(M-1,p), we find that

𝔼⁡[Zi​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(yi∣x)]=κ⁡(p)​∇θpθ​(C∣x),\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x)]=\kappa(p)\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}(C\mid x)\,,

where

κ⁡(t):=∑s=0M−1ϕs​(M−1s)​ts​(1−t)M−1−s.\kappa(t):=\sum_{s=0}^{M-1}\phi_{s}\binom{M-1}{s}t^{s}(1-t)^{M-1-s}.

Since dd​t​It​(s+1,M−s)=M​(M−1s)​ts​(1−t)M−1−s\frac{d}{dt}I_{t}(s+1,M-s)=M\binom{M-1}{s}t^{s}(1-t)^{M-1-s}, we have hM′​(t)=κ⁡(t)h_{M}^{\prime}(t)=\kappa(t), as desired.

In the next two sections, we consider the weights for rejection sampling and GRPO.

5 Rejection sampling

Consider the special case of Algorithm 1 (see e.g. Xiong et al. (2025)): Sample MM answers from the model, let VV denote the set of correct answers. Then use the gradient estimator:

1|V|​∑y∈V∇θ​log​πθ​(y∣x).\frac{1}{|V|}\sum_{y\in V}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x).

If you receive no correct answers, skip the step. One can see that the choice of advantage here is simply: Zi=Ri​M/(Si+1).Z_{i}=R_{i}M/(S_{i}+1). and thus, the induced cost function is:

hM​(t)=∑s=0M−11s+1​It​(s+1,M−s),h_{M}(t)=\sum_{s=0}^{M-1}\frac{1}{s+1}I_{t}(s+1,M-s),

Note that this function is close to log⁡(t)\log(t), and gets closer as MM approaches infinity. In fact, one can show that

hM​(t)=log⁡(t)+HM+∑r=M+1∞(1−t)rr,h_{M}(t)=\log(t)+H_{M}+\sum_{r=M+1}^{\infty}\frac{(1-t)^{r}}{r},

where HMH_{M} is the MMth harmonic number; see Figure 2.

One might wonder whether it’s possible to actually target the objective h⁡(t)=log⁡(t)h(t)=\log(t). This can be achieved by rejection sampling, which falls slightly outside of Algorithm 1. Indeed, consider the following algorithm:

  1. 1.

    Select a question from the corpus QQ.

  2. 2.

    For a chosen integer, BB, sample answers from the model until you observe BB correct responses. Let VV denote this set of correct answers.

  3. 3.

    Fine-tune the model with a supervised learning update

    θ←θ+η​1B​∑y∈V∇θ​log​πθ​(y|x).\theta\leftarrow\theta+\eta\frac{1}{B}\sum_{y\in V}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\,.

A similar algorithm using rejection sampling was proposed for post-training by Xiong et al. (2025). The algorithm as written here is in fact stochastic gradient ascent with an unbiased estimate of the gradient of JlogJ_{\log}. We use an analysis that mimics the log trick used to derive Williams’ REINFORCE algorithm. Note that

∇θ​log​∑y∈C⁡(x)πθ​(y|x)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\log\sum_{y\in C(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y|x) =∑y∈C⁡(x)∇θπθ​(y|x)∑y∈C⁡(x)πθ​(y|x)\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{y\in C(x)}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}{\sum_{y\in C(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}
=∑y∈C⁡(x)πθ​(y|x)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y|x)∑y∈C⁡(x)πθ​(y|x)\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{y\in C(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}{\sum_{y\in C(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}
=𝔼[∇θlogπθ(y|x)|y∈C(x),x].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)|y\in C(x),x]\,.

Hence, sampling yy using rejection sampling yields an unbiased stochastic gradient of the cost JlogJ_{\log}.

Note that this even gives a new way to implement supervised learning, albeit one that is not very practical. For a given example (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}), you can sample from yy from pθ(⋅|xi)p_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{i}) until you find one with y=yiy=y_{i}. At this point, update the model in the direction of the gradient of log⁡pθ​(y|xi)\log p_{\theta}(y|x_{i}). This algorithm maximizes the standard log-loss objective (2.1).

However, in the reinforcement learning context, the global objective JlogJ_{\log} does not have a natural interpretation as a maximum likelihood estimator unless there is a single correct answer in C⁡(x)C(x). The objective JlogJ_{\log} is more analogous to the multilabel problem in supervised learning where many labels can be counted as correct for a particular example data-point. As we discuss in the conclusion, it’s not clear whether there is a rigorous justification for using the logarithmic scaling in reinforcement learning contexts.

6 GRPO

The GRPO algorithm (Shao et al., 2024) is another renormalization of the sampled gradients. GRPO normalizes by the square root of the variance of the received rewards. This amplifies the impact of each update. Indeed, after sampling y1,…,yM∼πθ(⋅∣x)y_{1},\ldots,y_{M}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x), one forms the stochastic gradient estimator:

1M​∑i=1M(Ri−1M​∑i=1MRiVar⁡({Ri}i)+ε)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(yi|x)for some ε>0.\displaystyle\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\left(\frac{R_{i}-\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}R_{i}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\{R_{i}\}_{i})}+\varepsilon}\right)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}|x)\,\qquad\text{for some $\varepsilon>0$.} (6.1)

Which loss does this correspond to? Let us first note that conditioned on Si=sS_{i}=s, the weighting ZiZ_{i} is indeed linear in the indicator RiR_{i}

Zi:=Ri−1M​∑i=1MRiVar⁡({Ri}i)+ε=(1−Ri)​−qsqs​(1−qs)+ε+Ri​1−qs+1qs+1​(1−qs+1)+ε\displaystyle Z_{i}^{:}=\frac{R_{i}-\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}R_{i}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\{R_{i}\}_{i})}+\varepsilon}=(1-R_{i})\frac{-q_{s}}{\sqrt{q_{s}(1-q_{s})}+\varepsilon}+R_{i}\frac{1-q_{s+1}}{\sqrt{q_{s+1}(1-q_{s+1})}+\varepsilon}

where qs=s/Mq_{s}=s/M. From this expression, the objective induced by ZiZ_{i} is

JM,ε​(θ)=𝔼x∼Q​[hM,ε​(∑y∈C⁡(x)πθ​(y∣x))],J_{M,\varepsilon}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim Q}\left[h_{M,\varepsilon}\left(\sum_{y\in C(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\right)\right],

where hM,εh_{M,\varepsilon} is defined via (4.2):

hM,ε​(t):=1M​∑s=0M−1(1−qs+1qs+1​(1−qs+1)+ε+qsqs​(1−qs)+ε)​It​(s+1,M−s);\displaystyle h_{M,\varepsilon}(t):=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{s=0}^{M-1}\left(\frac{1-q_{s+1}}{\sqrt{q_{s+1}(1-q_{s+1})}+\varepsilon}+\frac{q_{s}}{\sqrt{q_{s}(1-q_{s})}+\varepsilon}\right)\,I_{t}(s+1,M-s);

This function is admittedly opaque, but one can get a sense of what it’s targeting by considering an idealized setting where ε=0\varepsilon=0 and we replace the sample mean and variance by their population values.

Indeed, let us consider the function h⁡(t)=2​arcsin⁡th(t)=2\arcsin\sqrt{t} and differentiate:

∇θh​(pθ​(C∣x))\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}h(p_{\theta}(C\mid x)) =∇θpθ​(C∣x)pθ​(C∣x)​(1−pθ​(C∣x))\displaystyle=\frac{\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}(C\mid x)}{\sqrt{p_{\theta}(C\mid x)(1-p_{\theta}(C\mid x))}}
=𝔼y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[R(y,x)∇θlogπθ(y∣x)]Vary∼πθ(⋅∣x)(R(y,x))\displaystyle=\dfrac{\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[R(y,x)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)]}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}(R(y,x))}}
=𝔼y∼πθ​(y∣x)​[(R(y,x)−𝔼y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[R(y,x)]Vary∼πθ(⋅∣x)(R(y,x)))​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y∣x)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}\left[\left(\dfrac{R(y,x)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[R(y,x)]}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}(R(y,x))}}\right)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\right],

where the third equality uses the fact that the expected value of the log derivative under πθ(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) is zero. Figure 3 plots the behavior of hM,ε/hM,ε​(1)h_{M,\varepsilon}/h_{M,\varepsilon}(1). Reassuringly, we see that for large MM and small ε\varepsilon, the function tends to h⁡(t)=2π​arcsin⁡th(t)=\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\sqrt{t}. As ε\varepsilon increases, hM,εh_{M,\varepsilon} behaves more like h⁡(t)=th(t)=t.

So again, like the rejection sampling algorithm from Section 5, the GRPO algorithm is optimizing a monotone rescaling of the probability of achieving a correct answer. Why is this a good scaling function? As we discuss in the conclusion, we’re not sure.

7 What do we learn?

This note only aims to provide language model researchers more clarity and flexibility in designing fine-tuning methods, so we provide no concrete recommendations. In fact, a variety of other sampling and reweighting methods can be derived using the approach of this note. For example, replacing the standard deviation by the variance in GRPO yields a function close to the log odds rescaling: h⁡(t)=log⁡(t/(1−t))h(t)=\log(t/(1-t)). Other rescalings based on normalizing by the pdf of the beta distribution have also been considered, e.g., in Xiao et al. (2025) and their associated loss functions which approximate the corresponding cdfs of the beta distribution can be deduced from 4.

What if maximizing log-odds is what you want? Or what if there’s some other scaling function hh you like? In that case, we can provide you a recipe for constructing a gradient estimator. The process is straightforward: the derivative of hMh_{M} in (4.2) is a Bernstein polynomial, which provides a basis in which to approximate any continuous function:

hM′​(t)=∑s=0M−1(bs−as)​(M−1s)​ts​(1−t)M−1−s\displaystyle h_{M}^{\prime}(t)\;=\;\sum_{s=0}^{M-1}(b_{s}-a_{s})\binom{M-1}{s}t^{s}(1-t)^{M-1-s} (7.1)

Then one simply needs to choose asa_{s} and bsb_{s} appropriately to best approximate h′h^{\prime} by hM′h_{M}^{\prime}. For example, if hh is a polynomial of degree ≤M\leq M, one may choose these coefficients so that hM′=h′h_{M}^{\prime}=h^{\prime} and hence hM=h+consth_{M}=h+\text{const}. If hh is an arbitrary smooth function, one can instead choose coefficients such that bs−as=h′​(s/(M−1))b_{s}-a_{s}=h^{\prime}\left(s/(M-1)\right). With this choice of coefficients, hMh_{M} converges uniformly to h+consth+\text{const} on [0,1][0,1]. One can even prove a rate of convergence if e.g., hh is CpC^{p} for p≥3p\geq 3. In this case the derivative hM′h_{M}^{\prime} converges in the sup\sup norm at a rate 1/M1/M, and the same result holds for hMh_{M} by the fundamental theorem of calculus (Adell and Cárdenas-Morales, 2022).

We do not see a reason to prefer any hh more than the identity. For a corpus consisting of a single question, each choice of h⁡(t)h(t) induces an identical problem, since hh is monotone. Unfortunately, it is hard to guess the practical effects of monotone rescaling of the objective function in this manner when there are multiple questions in the corpus. In fact, if we allow for an expressive enough representation of πθ\pi_{\theta} and globally maximize JhJ_{h}, the choice of hh is superfluous (though it may affect optimization dynamics): For any monotone scaling, the optimal choice is to place a total probability mass of 1 on C⁡(x)C(x) and 0 everywhere else. This is analogous to how hinge and logistic loss on linearly separable data are minimized at the same halfspaces.

Thus, arguing whether GRPO or REINFORCE is best is like arguing whether log loss is better than hinge loss for classification problems. There as well, Logistic regression and support vector machines differ only in a monotonic rescaling of errors in the objective function. Statistically, both return comparable classifiers with sufficient data (See, for example, Bartlett et al. (2006)). But neither loss has magical properties, and the best loss varies by task. In the same vein, the best rescaling for RL finetuning will be context dependent, since all such algorithms are chasing closely related objectives.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
